title: Design a URL Shortener (like Bit.ly)
functional: Create a short URL for a long URL (optional custom alias)
Redirect a short URL to the original URL
Optional expiry for links
Basic click analytics per link
nonFunctional: Redirect latency under ~50 ms at p99
Highly available redirects (reads matter more than writes)
Short codes must be unique and hard to guess sequentially
scale: 100M new URLs/month, read:write ratio about 100:1 (~4K redirects/s average, 10x at peak), store links for 5 years (~6B rows).
keyComponents: Stateless API servers behind a load balancer
ID generator (counter ranges or Snowflake) + base62 encoding
Cache (Redis) in front of the store for hot links
deepDives: How do you generate unique short codes without collisions or a single point of failure?
301 vs 302 redirects — what is the trade-off for analytics and caching?
How do you handle a viral link that suddenly gets millions of hits?
How do you delete expired links efficiently?
referenceDesign: Write path: API validates the URL, gets a unique 64-bit ID from pre-allocated counter ranges (each app server leases a block from ZooKeeper/DB) or a Snowflake-style generator, base62-encodes it to ~7 chars, and stores code -> {longUrl, userId, expiresAt} in a horizontally partitioned KV store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) keyed by code. Read path: check Redis (LRU, 20% of hot links cover most traffic), fall back to the KV store, return 302 so clicks can be counted (301 lets browsers cache but loses analytics). Clicks are emitted to Kafka and aggregated asynchronously. Expiry via TTL columns plus lazy check on read. Custom aliases use a conditional put to detect conflicts.
pitfalls: Using an MD5 hash prefix without handling collisions
Counting clicks synchronously on the redirect path
A single auto-increment DB as the only ID source

title: Design Pastebin
functional: Users paste text and get a unique link
Anyone with the link can view the paste
Pastes can expire (10 min, 1 day, never)
Optional syntax highlighting and private pastes
scale: 1M new pastes/day, 10M reads/day, average paste 10 KB (~3.6 TB/year of content).
keyComponents: Metadata DB (key, owner, expiry, size, content pointer)
deepDives: Why separate content (object storage) from metadata (DB)?
How do you pre-generate keys so writes never collide?
How does expiry cleanup work at scale without hurting read traffic?
referenceDesign: Keys are pre-generated by a Key Generation Service into an 'unused' table and handed out in batches to app servers. Content is written to S3 under the key; metadata row stores the S3 path, expiry and visibility. Reads hit a CDN/Redis first, then metadata DB + S3. Expired pastes are filtered on read and deleted by a periodic batch job scanning an expiry index. Rate limiting per IP prevents abuse.
pitfalls: Storing multi-MB blobs directly in a relational DB
No abuse/rate limiting on anonymous writes

title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
functional: Limit requests per client (user ID, API key, or IP) per time window
Different rules per endpoint (e.g. login 5/min, search 100/min)
Return HTTP 429 with retry information when throttled
Rules can be changed without redeploying
nonFunctional: Adds under 1–2 ms latency per request
Works across many API servers (shared state)
Fails open or closed deliberately if the limiter store is down
scale: Global API handling 1M requests/s across hundreds of servers, 50M distinct clients.
keyComponents: Limiter middleware in the API gateway
Redis cluster storing counters/buckets with TTL
Local in-memory pre-check for very hot keys
deepDives: Compare fixed window, sliding log, sliding window counter and token bucket — which do you pick and why?
How do you avoid race conditions when many servers update the same counter?
What happens if Redis is slow or unavailable?
How do you rate limit across multiple data centers?
referenceDesign: Middleware in the gateway computes a key (clientId:endpoint) and runs an atomic Lua script in Redis implementing token bucket or sliding-window-counter (INCR + EXPIRE, or two windows weighted). Redis is sharded by key hash; rules are cached locally and refreshed from a config service. Responses include X-RateLimit-Remaining/Retry-After. For multi-region, limit locally per region with a slightly lower budget or use eventually-consistent sync. On Redis failure, fail open for normal endpoints and fail closed for sensitive ones like login.
pitfalls: Read-then-write counter updates (race conditions) instead of atomic operations
Fixed windows allowing 2x burst at boundaries without acknowledging it

title: Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator
functional: Generate globally unique 64-bit numeric IDs
IDs are roughly time-ordered
Many services call it concurrently
nonFunctional: IDs never repeat even after restarts
scale: Hundreds of services, peak 1M IDs/s cluster-wide.
deepDives: Compare UUIDs, DB auto-increment with step, ticket servers and Snowflake.
How do you handle the clock moving backwards?
How are worker IDs assigned and reclaimed safely?
referenceDesign: Snowflake layout: 1 sign bit, 41 bits millisecond timestamp since a custom epoch (~69 years), 10 bits worker ID (5 datacenter + 5 machine), 12 bits sequence (4096 IDs/ms/node). Worker IDs are leased from ZooKeeper at startup. If the clock goes backwards, the node waits until it catches up or refuses to issue IDs and alerts. Sequence resets each millisecond; if exhausted, spin to the next ms.
pitfalls: Choosing UUIDv4 without discussing index fragmentation and lack of ordering
Ignoring clock skew

title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store (like DynamoDB)
functional: put(key, value) and get(key)
Values up to 1 MB
Tunable consistency per request
nonFunctional: Always writable (high availability) and partition tolerant
scale: 10 PB of data, 1M operations/s, thousands of nodes across 3 regions.
keyComponents: Consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes
Vector clocks or last-write-wins for conflicts
LSM-tree storage engine (memtable, SSTables, bloom filters)
deepDives: How does consistent hashing minimize data movement when nodes join or leave?
Explain how R + W > N gives strong consistency and what you lose.
How do you detect and repair diverged replicas?
Walk through the write path down to disk.
referenceDesign: Keys are hashed onto a ring with virtual nodes for balance; each key is stored on the next N=3 distinct physical nodes. A coordinator handles each request, writing to N replicas and succeeding after W acks (reads wait for R). With W=R=2, N=3 reads see the latest write. Temporarily failed replicas are covered by hinted handoff; permanent divergence is repaired by comparing Merkle trees. Membership spreads by gossip; failure detection by heartbeat suspicion. Conflicts resolved by vector clocks (client merge) or LWW timestamps. Storage engine: commit log + memtable flushed to SSTables, bloom filters and compaction.
pitfalls: Modulo hashing (rehashes everything on resize)
Claiming strong consistency and 100% availability during partitions

title: Design a Distributed Cache (like Redis/Memcached cluster)
functional: get/set/delete with TTL
LRU (or LFU) eviction when memory is full
Cluster scales by adding nodes
nonFunctional: Cache can be lost without losing source-of-truth data
scale: 1 TB of hot data, 2M requests/s, 95%+ hit rate target.
keyComponents: Cache nodes (hash map + doubly linked list for LRU)
deepDives: Cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind — when to use each?
How do you handle a hot key that overloads one shard?
How do you prevent a cache stampede when a popular key expires?
How do you keep cache and database consistent on updates?
referenceDesign: Clients route keys via consistent hashing to shards; each shard is a primary with async replicas for failover (Sentinel-style). Node internals: hash map + doubly linked list gives O(1) LRU. Use cache-aside for most reads: on miss read DB, populate with TTL; on update write DB then delete the cache key. Stampede protection with request coalescing / locks and jittered TTLs. Hot keys: replicate to multiple shards with a suffix or add a local in-process cache.
pitfalls: Updating the cache before the DB (stale data on failure)
Identical TTLs causing synchronized expiry storms

title: Design a Notification System (push, SMS, email)
functional: Send push (iOS/Android), SMS and email notifications
Triggered by services or scheduled campaigns
Respect user preferences and opt-outs
Track delivery status
scale: 10M push, 1M SMS and 5M emails per day, bursts during campaigns.
deepDives: Why one queue per channel?
How do you guarantee at-least-once delivery without spamming duplicates?
How do you throttle so a user isn't flooded?
What happens when a third-party provider is down?
referenceDesign: Services call the Notification API, which checks preferences and rate limits, renders templates, and enqueues one message per channel with an idempotency key. Channel workers pull from their queue and call providers; failures are retried with exponential backoff, then moved to a DLQ. A dedup store (key with TTL) prevents duplicate sends. Delivery status is written to a log for analytics. Scheduled campaigns are fanned out by a scheduler in batches to smooth load.
pitfalls: Calling providers synchronously in the request path
No idempotency — retries cause duplicate notifications

title: Design a Social Media News Feed (like Facebook/Twitter)
functional: Users publish posts (text, images)
Users see a feed of posts from people they follow, newest or ranked
Like and comment counts shown on posts
nonFunctional: Posting is fast; feed can be slightly stale (eventual consistency)
Handles celebrities with millions of followers
scale: 300M DAU, each opens the feed 10x/day (~35K feed reads/s), 1 post/user/day, average 200 follows.
keyComponents: Feed cache per user (list of post IDs)
deepDives: Push (fan-out on write) vs pull (fan-out on read) — how do you handle celebrities?
What exactly is stored in the feed cache?
How do you paginate a feed that changes while scrolling?
How is ranking added without hurting latency?
referenceDesign: On post, store it, then enqueue fan-out: workers fetch follower IDs and prepend the post ID into each follower's Redis feed list (capped at ~800). For celebrities (>~10K followers) skip fan-out; their posts are pulled and merged at read time (hybrid). Feed read: get post IDs from cache, hydrate posts/users from caches, merge celebrity posts, rank, return with a cursor (last post ID/timestamp). Media served from CDN. Counters stored separately and updated asynchronously.
pitfalls: Pure fan-out on write (celebrity post = millions of writes)
Offset-based pagination on a live feed

title: Design a Chat System (like WhatsApp/Messenger)
functional: 1:1 and group chats (up to 500 members)
Online/offline presence and last seen
Message history synced across devices
Delivery and read receipts
nonFunctional: Messages never lost; ordered within a conversation
Supports hundreds of millions of concurrent connections
scale: 500M DAU, 40 messages/user/day (~230K messages/s average), 100M concurrent connections.
keyComponents: Chat servers holding persistent WebSocket connections
Message service + wide-column store (Cassandra/HBase) partitioned by conversation
Push notification service for offline users
deepDives: How does a message reach a user connected to a different chat server?
How do you guarantee ordering and no duplicates?
How does a user who was offline get missed messages on reconnect?
How does group chat fan-out differ from 1:1?
referenceDesign: Clients hold a WebSocket to a chat server (chosen by a service-discovery layer). Sending: server assigns a per-conversation monotonically increasing ID, persists to the message store (partition key = conversation ID, clustering = message ID), acks the sender, then looks up recipients' servers in the registry and forwards via an internal pub/sub; offline recipients get a push notification. Each device keeps the max message ID it has seen and syncs newer ones on reconnect. Presence uses heartbeats with a timeout and publishes changes only to friends. Group messages fan out to member inboxes (small groups) with delivery receipts aggregated.
pitfalls: HTTP polling at this scale
Relying on client timestamps for ordering

title: Design Search Autocomplete (Typeahead)
functional: Return top 5 suggestions for a typed prefix
Suggestions ranked by popularity (and recency)
Filter offensive terms
nonFunctional: Suggestions can lag reality by minutes/hours
scale: 10M DAU, 10 searches/day, ~20 characters each → ~24K requests/s (keystroke-driven).
keyComponents: Trie with top-k cached at each node
deepDives: Why store the top-k at each trie node?
How is the trie rebuilt and deployed without downtime?
How do you shard the trie when it doesn't fit on one machine?
How do you reduce requests per keystroke?
referenceDesign: Query logs flow into a batch/streaming aggregator computing frequencies. A builder creates a trie where each node stores its top-5 completions, serialized and loaded into trie servers (sharded by first characters, balanced by historical load), swapped atomically after rebuild. Requests: client debounces keystrokes, server does an O(prefix length) lookup and returns cached top-k; responses cached in browser for short TTL. Filtering layer removes blocked terms. Trending terms can be merged from a real-time stream.
pitfalls: Traversing the whole subtree per request to find top-k
Updating the trie synchronously on every search

title: Design a Video Streaming Platform (like YouTube/Netflix)
functional: Upload videos
Stream videos smoothly on many devices and networks
Search and view metadata (title, views, likes)
nonFunctional: Fast playback start and minimal buffering worldwide
scale: 5M DAU watching 5 videos/day, 10% upload 1 video/day (~150 MB each) → ~75 TB new raw video/day before transcoding.
keyComponents: Upload service with pre-signed URLs + resumable multipart upload
Transcoding pipeline (DAG of tasks on workers via queue)
deepDives: Walk through the transcoding pipeline and how it scales.
How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?
How do you decide what goes on the CDN vs origin?
How are view counts updated at huge scale?
referenceDesign: Client gets a pre-signed URL and uploads directly to blob storage in resumable chunks. An upload-complete event triggers the transcoding DAG: split into segments, encode to multiple bitrates/codecs in parallel, generate thumbnails, package as HLS/DASH manifests. Outputs go to storage and are pushed/pulled by the CDN (popular content cached at edges; long tail served from regional origins). Players fetch a manifest and switch bitrate per segment based on bandwidth. Metadata in a sharded DB with caches; views counted via streaming aggregation.
pitfalls: Uploading video through application servers
Serving everything from CDN regardless of popularity (cost)

title: Design Google Drive / Dropbox
functional: Upload, download and delete files
Sync files across a user's devices
File version history
Share files with other users
nonFunctional: Efficient sync of large files over slow networks
scale: 50M users, 10M DAU, 15 GB quota each, ~2 uploads/user/day.
keyComponents: Metadata DB (files, versions, blocks, users) — relational
Offline backup/cold storage for old versions
deepDives: Why split files into chunks and hash them?
How does a device learn another device changed a file?
What happens when two devices edit the same file offline?
How do you keep metadata strongly consistent at scale?
referenceDesign: Client splits files into ~4 MB blocks, hashes each (SHA-256), asks the server which blocks are missing, and uploads only those (delta sync + dedup across users). Metadata (file -> ordered block hashes, version) is committed in a relational DB transaction after blocks are stored. Other devices hold a long-poll/WebSocket to the notification service and fetch changed metadata, then download missing blocks. Conflicts: first commit wins; the other client's version is saved as a 'conflicted copy'. Old versions kept by reference to blocks; cold blocks moved to cheaper storage.
pitfalls: Re-uploading whole files on every change
Eventually consistent metadata store causing lost updates

title: Design a Web Crawler
functional: Crawl the web starting from seed URLs
Download and store HTML pages
Extract links and discover new pages
Re-crawl pages periodically
nonFunctional: Politeness: don't overload any single host, respect robots.txt
Robust to traps, bad HTML and slow servers
scale: 1B pages/month (~400 pages/s), average page 500 KB → ~500 TB/month.
deepDives: How does the frontier enforce politeness and priority at the same time?
How do you avoid crawling the same URL or duplicate content?
How do you detect spider traps?
How do you distribute the crawl across machines?
referenceDesign: Frontier has front queues by priority (PageRank/freshness) and back queues mapped one-per-host, each with a next-allowed-fetch time, so a worker only takes a host when its delay has elapsed. Workers resolve DNS via a local cache, fetch with timeouts, respect robots.txt (cached), and store pages. Parsed links are normalized, checked against a Bloom filter of seen URLs, and enqueued. Content fingerprints (SimHash) catch near-duplicates. URLs are partitioned by host hash across crawler nodes. Depth limits and URL length limits defend against traps.
pitfalls: A single FIFO queue that hammers one host
Keeping all seen URLs in a hash set in memory

title: Design a Ride-Sharing Service (like Uber/Lyft)
functional: Riders request a ride and see nearby drivers
Match a rider with a nearby available driver
Real-time driver location tracking during the trip
Fare estimation and payment at the end
nonFunctional: A driver must never be assigned to two riders
Location updates handled at high write volume
scale: 100M riders, 1M active drivers sending location every 4 s (~250K writes/s).
keyComponents: Location service (drivers stream GPS via WebSocket)
deepDives: How do you find the nearest available drivers quickly?
How do you avoid double-booking a driver?
How do you store and process 250K location updates per second?
How does surge pricing work?
referenceDesign: Drivers send location over WebSockets to location servers that update an in-memory geo index (geohash cells -> driver sets, Redis GEO) with TTL; history goes to a stream for analytics. Ride request: matching service queries nearby cells, ranks candidates by ETA, and offers the ride to one driver at a time with a short timeout. Assignment uses a lock/compare-and-set on driver status to prevent double booking. Trip lifecycle (requested → accepted → in-progress → completed) persisted in a sharded DB. Surge: demand/supply ratio per cell computed in near real-time.
pitfalls: Querying a relational DB with lat/lng ranges for every request
No atomic driver state change (double dispatch)

title: Design a Proximity Service (like Yelp nearby search)
functional: Return businesses within a radius of the user's location
Business owners add/update listings (not real-time)
View business details
nonFunctional: Updates may appear the next day
scale: 100M DAU, 5 searches/day (~5K QPS), 200M businesses.
keyComponents: Geospatial index (geohash table or in-memory quadtree)
Cache for business details and geohash cells
deepDives: Compare geohash, quadtree and S2/H3 for this use case.
How do you handle searches near cell boundaries?
How do you scale reads?
referenceDesign: Businesses indexed by geohash (precision chosen by radius, e.g. 6 chars ≈ 1.2 km). Query: compute user's geohash plus its 8 neighbors to avoid boundary misses, fetch business IDs from a geohash -> IDs table (or cache), filter by exact distance, rank, hydrate details from cache. The dataset fits in memory, so read replicas/cache scale reads easily. Updates written to primary DB and index rebuilt nightly.
pitfalls: Forgetting neighbor cells at geohash boundaries
Real-time index updates when the requirements allow daily ones

title: Design a Distributed Message Queue (like Kafka)
functional: Producers publish messages to topics
Consumers subscribe and read in order within a partition
Messages retained for a configurable period
Consumers can replay from an offset
scale: 1M messages/s, 1 KB average, 7-day retention (~600 TB).
keyComponents: Brokers storing partitions as segmented append-only logs
Leader/follower replication with in-sync replica set
deepDives: Why is an append-only log on disk so fast?
How does replication work and what does acks=all guarantee?
How are partitions assigned to consumers and rebalanced?
How do you achieve exactly-once processing?
referenceDesign: Topics are split into partitions; each partition is an ordered log split into segment files with an offset index, written sequentially and read via page cache/zero-copy. Each partition has a leader and followers; followers fetch from the leader, and acks=all waits for the in-sync replicas. Producers batch and compress, choosing a partition by key hash to keep per-key ordering. Consumer groups divide partitions among members; offsets are committed to an internal topic. Exactly-once via idempotent producers (sequence numbers) + transactions. Retention deletes old segments or compacts by key.
pitfalls: Promising global ordering across partitions
Committing offsets before processing (message loss)

title: Design a Metrics Monitoring and Alerting System
functional: Collect metrics (CPU, latency, error rates) from thousands of servers
Query and visualize metrics on dashboards
Alert via email/Slack/PagerDuty when rules fire
nonFunctional: Handles high write volume with low query latency on recent data
Alerting must stay reliable even under load
scale: 100K servers × 100 metrics every 10 s → 1M data points/s.
keyComponents: Collection agents (pull by scraper or push to gateway)
deepDives: Pull vs push collection — trade-offs?
Why a time-series DB instead of a relational DB?
How do you avoid alert storms and duplicate pages?
How is old data downsampled?
referenceDesign: Agents expose metrics that scrapers pull (service discovery) or push via a gateway into Kafka. Consumers write to a TSDB that stores series by metric+labels with delta-of-delta/gorilla compression and an inverted index on tags. Recent data kept hot in memory. Dashboards query via a query layer with caching. Alert evaluator runs rules on intervals, and an alert manager groups, dedupes and routes notifications with silencing. Background jobs roll up raw data into 1m/1h aggregates for long retention.
pitfalls: Storing every data point in a normalized SQL table
High-cardinality labels (user IDs) exploding series count

title: Design an Ad Click Event Aggregation System
functional: Count clicks per ad over the last N minutes
Return top 100 most-clicked ads per minute
Support filtering by region, device, etc.
nonFunctional: Aggregation latency of a few minutes
scale: 1B clicks/day (~10K/s average, 50K/s peak), 2M ads.
deepDives: Event time vs processing time — how do you handle late events (watermarks)?
How do you avoid double counting on failures?
How do you compute top-k efficiently?
How do you verify results are correct?
referenceDesign: Clicks are appended to Kafka partitioned by ad ID. Flink consumes with event-time tumbling 1-minute windows and watermarks allowing a few minutes of lateness; state checkpointing + transactional sinks give exactly-once. Deduplicate by click ID. Per-minute counts and a top-k (heap per partition, merged) are written to an OLAP store for queries. Raw events land in cheap storage; a daily batch recomputes and reconciles with streaming results for billing accuracy.
pitfalls: Processing-time windows (wrong counts under lag)
No reconciliation for money-related numbers

title: Design a Hotel Reservation System (like Booking.com)
functional: Search hotels and see room availability for dates
Reserve a room type for a date range
Cancel a reservation
Support overbooking up to a configured percentage
nonFunctional: No double booking beyond allowed overbooking
Correctness over raw throughput for bookings
scale: 5,000 hotels, 1M rooms, ~3 reservations/s average (read traffic much higher).
keyComponents: Inventory table (hotel, room type, date, total, reserved)
deepDives: How do you model inventory so availability checks are cheap?
How do you prevent two users booking the last room at the same time?
How do you make the reserve API idempotent against double clicks?
referenceDesign: Inventory stored per (hotel_id, room_type_id, date) with total and reserved counts. Reservation: in one transaction, check all dates satisfy reserved + 1 <= total × 1.1 and increment, using optimistic locking (version column) or a DB constraint; conditional updates beat pessimistic locks at this QPS. The client generates a reservation ID (idempotency key) so retries don't double book. Search served from cache/read replicas; the authoritative check happens at booking time.
pitfalls: Checking availability and booking in separate non-atomic steps
Using distributed locks when a DB constraint suffices

title: Design a Payment System
functional: Customers pay for orders via a payment service provider (Stripe/Adyen)
Pay out to sellers
Refunds
Track status of every payment
nonFunctional: Never charge twice; never lose money
Handle PSP timeouts and retries safely
scale: 1M transactions/day (~10 TPS) — correctness, not throughput, is the challenge.
keyComponents: Reconciliation jobs against PSP settlement files
deepDives: How do you guarantee exactly-once charging with retries?
Why use a double-entry ledger?
How do you handle an ambiguous PSP timeout?
How is reconciliation done?
referenceDesign: Checkout creates a payment order with a unique idempotency key (also sent to the PSP). Hosted payment page keeps card data out of our systems (PCI). Payment state machine persisted in a DB; PSP result arrives via webhook and is recorded idempotently. On success the ledger writes balanced debit/credit entries in one transaction and wallets update. Timeouts leave payments 'pending' and are resolved by querying the PSP, never by blind retries without the idempotency key. Nightly reconciliation compares ledger vs PSP settlement files and flags mismatches.
pitfalls: Retrying charges without idempotency keys
Mutable balance columns without a ledger

title: Design an Event Ticket Booking System (like Ticketmaster)
functional: Browse events and seat maps
Hold selected seats for a few minutes during checkout
Complete purchase and receive tickets
Release seats if checkout isn't completed
nonFunctional: Survive flash-sale spikes (millions of users at on-sale time)
Fair ordering for users in the queue
scale: Popular on-sale: 10M users hitting at once for 50K seats.
keyComponents: Event/venue service + CDN for static seat maps
Virtual waiting room / queue with admission tokens
deepDives: How do you implement temporary seat holds that expire?
How do you stop 10M users from crushing the booking service?
How do you guarantee no double selling?
referenceDesign: At on-sale, users enter a virtual waiting room and are admitted at a controlled rate via signed tokens. Seat hold: atomic conditional update (status AVAILABLE → HELD with holdUntil and userId) or Redis SET NX with TTL; holds expire automatically. Checkout completes payment then marks seats SOLD in a transaction that checks the hold is still owned by the user. Seat maps and event pages cached on CDN; availability updates pushed or polled.
pitfalls: Letting all users hit the booking DB simultaneously
Holding seats without expiry

title: Design an E-commerce Platform (like Amazon) — catalog, cart and checkout
functional: Browse and search products
Add items to cart
Checkout: reserve inventory, pay, create order
Order status tracking
nonFunctional: Catalog and search highly available and fast
Checkout must be reliable even if one service fails
scale: 50M DAU, 200M products, 1M orders/day with 10x spikes on sale days.
deepDives: How do you keep search in sync with the catalog?
How do you avoid overselling during a flash sale?
How do you coordinate order, inventory and payment without distributed transactions?
referenceDesign: Catalog in a document store, replicated to Elasticsearch via change events; heavy caching and CDN for images. Cart in a KV store keyed by user. Checkout runs a saga: reserve inventory (conditional decrement with a reservation TTL), charge payment, confirm order; failure at any step triggers compensations (release inventory, refund). Events flow over Kafka; each service owns its DB. Order status updates are pushed to users.
pitfalls: A single two-phase commit across all services
Decrementing stock at add-to-cart time

title: Design a Photo Sharing App (like Instagram)
functional: Upload photos with captions
Follow users and view a home feed
Like and comment on photos
View a user's profile grid
nonFunctional: Feed loads fast; uploads can be processed asynchronously
scale: 500M users, 100M DAU, 50M photo uploads/day (~2 MB each → 100 TB/day raw).
deepDives: How do uploads and resizing work without blocking the user?
How do you shard photo metadata?
How do you build the home feed?
How do you store like counts for viral photos?
referenceDesign: Clients upload directly to object storage via pre-signed URLs; an event triggers workers to generate sizes and write metadata (photo ID from Snowflake, sharded by user ID). Images served via CDN. Home feed uses hybrid fan-out as in a news feed. Likes are stored as rows (user, photo) for dedup while counts are aggregated in a counter service (sharded counters / async batching). Profile grid read by user shard with pagination.
pitfalls: Serving images from app servers
Row-per-like counts computed with COUNT(*) on read

title: Design a Distributed Job Scheduler (like cron at scale)
functional: Schedule one-off and recurring (cron) jobs
Execute jobs on a worker fleet
Retry failed jobs with backoff
View job status and history
nonFunctional: Jobs start within a few seconds of their scheduled time
No job lost; duplicates minimized and tolerated via idempotency
Scales to millions of scheduled jobs
scale: 10M scheduled jobs, 10K executions/s at peak minutes.
keyComponents: Next-run index partitioned by time bucket
Scheduler nodes (partition ownership via leader election/leases)
deepDives: How do schedulers find due jobs without scanning everything?
How do you prevent two schedulers firing the same job?
What happens if a worker dies mid-job?
referenceDesign: Jobs stored with next_run_time; an index keyed by time bucket (minute) and shard lets each scheduler poll only its partitions for due jobs. Partition ownership is coordinated through leases in etcd/ZooKeeper. Due jobs are claimed with a conditional update (status SCHEDULED → QUEUED, version check) and pushed to a queue; workers ack on completion and use visibility timeouts so crashed jobs are redelivered. Recurring jobs compute and store the next run on completion. Jobs must be idempotent since delivery is at-least-once.
pitfalls: A single scheduler node (SPOF)
Full-table scans for due jobs every second

title: Design a Real-Time Gaming Leaderboard
functional: Update a player's score when they win a match
Show the top 10 players
Show a player's rank and nearby players
scale: 25M monthly active players, 50M score updates/day (~2.5K/s peak).
deepDives: Why is a relational ORDER BY query a problem here?
How do you scale beyond one Redis node?
How do you get a player's rank quickly?
referenceDesign: Store scores in a Redis sorted set per leaderboard period: ZINCRBY on win, ZREVRANGE 0 9 for top 10, ZREVRANK + ZREVRANGE around the rank for neighbors — all O(log n). Scores also written to a durable DB for recovery. If one node isn't enough, shard by score range (fixed partitions) or by user hash with scatter-gather for top-k. New month = new key.
pitfalls: Recomputing ranks with SQL on every request

title: Design a Collaborative Document Editor (like Google Docs)
functional: Multiple users edit the same document simultaneously
See others' cursors and changes in real time
Document history and restore
Comments and sharing permissions
nonFunctional: Edits appear to collaborators within ~100 ms
All users converge to the same document
No lost edits, works offline briefly
scale: 10M DAU, typical document has 1–10 concurrent editors, hot docs up to 100.
deepDives: Compare OT and CRDTs.
Why route all editors of a document to the same server?
How do you store history efficiently?
How do offline edits merge back?
referenceDesign: All clients of a document connect (via consistent hashing on doc ID) to the collaboration server owning that doc. Clients send operations tagged with the revision they're based on; the server transforms them against concurrent ops (OT), assigns a new revision, appends to the op log and broadcasts. Snapshots are taken every N ops so loading = snapshot + tail of ops. CRDTs are an alternative allowing peer/offline merges without a central transformer at the cost of metadata overhead. Presence (cursors) is ephemeral and broadcast without persistence.
pitfalls: Last-write-wins on whole documents
Letting editors of one doc connect to different uncoordinated servers

title: Design an API Gateway
functional: Route external requests to the right microservice
Authenticate and authorize requests
Rate limit per client
Request/response transformation and aggregation
nonFunctional: Highly available — it's on every request path
scale: 500K requests/s across 200 backend services.
keyComponents: Stateless gateway nodes behind L4 load balancers
Routing config store with hot reload
deepDives: How do you update routing rules without restarts?
How do circuit breakers protect the system?
How do you avoid the gateway becoming a bottleneck or SPOF?
referenceDesign: Gateway nodes are stateless and horizontally scaled behind an L4 LB; routing tables are pushed from a config service and swapped atomically. Auth validates JWTs locally using cached public keys. Rate limiting via a shared Redis with local token caches. Per-backend circuit breakers, timeouts and bounded retries with jitter; bulkheads isolate connection pools. Every request gets a trace ID; metrics and logs go to the observability stack.
pitfalls: Putting business logic in the gateway
Unlimited retries amplifying outages

title: Design a Food Delivery Platform (like DoorDash/Swiggy)
functional: Browse nearby restaurants and menus
Place and pay for an order
Restaurant accepts and prepares; a courier is assigned
Live order and courier tracking
scale: 20M orders/day at peak dinner hours (~1K orders/s), 500K active couriers sending GPS.
deepDives: How is the courier chosen (distance, ETA, batching orders)?
How do you model order states and handle cancellations?
How is live tracking delivered to customers efficiently?
referenceDesign: Restaurants indexed geographically with menus cached. Placing an order creates it in PLACED state, authorizes payment and notifies the restaurant; transitions (ACCEPTED, PREPARING, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED) are validated by a state machine and emitted as events. Dispatch picks couriers using predicted food-ready time, courier ETA and possible batching, offering to one courier at a time with timeouts. Courier GPS flows into a location service; customers subscribe to their order's channel over WebSockets.
pitfalls: Assigning a courier the moment the order is placed regardless of prep time
